fileDesc.titleStmt: CORRESPONDENCE OF THE FOUNDLING HOSPITAL INSPECTORS IN BERKSHIRE 1757-68. ED. BY GILLIAN CLARK. BERKSHIRE RECORD SOCIETY VOL. 1. 1994.

text.p: December 4th 1758
Madam

I rec'd the linen you sent by the waggon with the three bodice coats, without the two blankets and clouts which I desired for Jho Wigmore, No 6097, above a year old, or any reason for not sending them.

The bearer hereof, being come for a child, I take this opportunity of desiring you to send me down by her (if you have them ready) to save carriage, one bodice coat for Those Orange, No 5010, and one for Jho Wigmore, No 6097, also one bodice coat more and two pincloths for Ann Drummond, No 5644, all of them above a year old. If you can't send them by the bearer, please to forward them by the Oakingham Waggon the first opportunity. Ann Lewis, who brought up the poor disturbed baby to the hospital, says you then promised her another dry child when it suited her to take one. And now that unhappy babe is dead, she send her duty to you and desire the favour of another and that you would please to let her know when to come up for one.

Please to acquaint the hospital that Mary Blagrove, the nurse of the pocky child, who was thought out of danger, hath of late had very bad symptoms
and that Dr Musket hath put her into a course of mercurial physic and saith, if that don't do, she must be salivated; but I hope there will be no occasion for it, as she sent me word a few days ago she thought the physic had done her good.
The Hughes
Oakm, January 15th 1759
Sr

I am ordered by the Reverend Mr Penington to make up the account relating to the Foundling Hospital and send them which you have herewith, which I hope will be found wright and satisfactory. If any thing be not clear, please to give me an account and I shall endeavour to set it clear. If anything is done
contrary to the rules of the hospital, please to inform me. Relating to the expenses of the children, according to your request, have sent Mr Wheeler's bill for the cure of Nurse Deane and attendance of the children under her care. The reason of too apothecaries is Nurse Deane chose Dr Wheeler as being the apothecary she had some times applied to. Please to let me know if I should pay Mr Wheeler's bill or what part of it. If the governors please to allow her something for her loss of time, as I mentioned before, by seeing the bill they may judge her case. Inform me what I am to do. Likewise, you have the account from South Morton of the children under Mr Penington's inspection their. Please to send some blank receipts as soon as convenient. The child Constance Jackson, No 10378, died Decr 25th with convulsions and the child Anne Henderson, No 9958, died Decr 9th with convulsions. Have herewith sent their clothes.

The shows may be thought dear; the were ordered by Mr Penington to be made at Oakingham, as he thought for the best, to be strong, but I find it will not do for them. The being strong, the childreen outgrow them and they are not wore out. That shows at 9d or 10d will answer better, Mr Penington ordered me to inform that, when letters come from the hospital, you'll please to direct to me as Mr Penington is at 25 miles distance from Oakingham and is attended with much trouble sending to and from Morton as it being out of any high road. I am, sr, for the Revd Mr Penington, Your most obdient Humle st
J. Buns
Oakm, October 15th 1759
Sr

On the other side you have the account relating to the children of the Foundling Hospital under the inspection of the Revd Mr Penington, both at Wokingham and at Morton, Barks. Likewise you have herewith the No 6573. The child died Aug 19th of consumption and No 7896, the child died Augt 26th of consumption. The clothes are kept for others that will want. No 13739, the child died Sept 3rd of fits. You have the clothes herewith. Likewise the clothes which Mr Penington sent me from Morton I have sent to you. Desire to have blank receipts sent by waggon as it is very ilconvenient to pay the nurses without them and causes much trouble. Hope the accts will be found wright. It may be asked why the shows should not be all of a price, to which I answer: them at 12d a pare are which we call homemade for strength, the others were sale shows and did not do but very little service. Likewise why the funeral expenses should be more than last year: to that, the officers of the parish have insisted on my causing an affidavit to be made, which was not done last year.

Mr Penington desired me to write my opinion on allowing the nurses 3d per week for clothing as I am much more acquainted with the nurses then him. The are all willing to comply with the rules of the hospital so far as to try what the can do for the money, but I am fearful it will be much more trouble to the inspectors then now. I am doubtful whether many will not neglect to layout the 3d per week for clothes for the pore children, but make them suffer with cold for want of clothes, as many of their own do, whereas the do now keep them warm and clean with what clothes is allowed them. Which if they should neglect them, it wold cause much more trouble to see the are provided with nessesaryes, and may then be imposed on by their saying shush and shush things belong to the Foundling. At the same time it may near all belong to their own children and that they have scarce any
thing to were but now when I have visited them, find them well clothed. Hope you'll excuse the freedom I have taken in declaring my sentiments on this head, as I shall be willing to comply to rules. For the Revd Mr Penington.
J. Buns, Assistant to Mr Penington

note.value: MR J. BUNCE, WOKINGHAM, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Oakm, December 23rd 1759
Sr

Yours of the eighteenth int I rec'd. Persuant to your request have, I believe, engaged about 6 nurses which shall be at the hospital Friday evening next. Will it be possible, send more. Desire the may have strong children delivered to them as the come more at my request then of there own inclination, but know them to be good wet nurses as the most all have foundlings already. Sr, should take it as a favour if you cold deliver too dry nurse children to too good dry nurses which I cold send, as Mr Penington have not had every one at Wokingham since he had the management of them. Hope it is to be his turn by this time, or if it be but one, please to give me a sine per return of post and can forward a dry nurse with the wet nurse, as too dry nurses, which will be more agreeable.
J. Buns, Asst

note.value: MR J. BUNCE, WOKINGHAM, 1759 TO THE SECRETARY
TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Oakingham, December 28th 1759
Sr

The child James Creed, No 13684, is removed by the desire of the nurse to Ann Grout, De'r 21st. The child Jo Brombley, No 14336, died Nov'r 24th of a fit and the child Ed Cranmer, 14473, died Dec'r 22 of Ditto . The clothes I have returned per the nurses. I have sent my own team to bring those nurses as wold not come to be out so long as the common stage generally is. Please to let them have the children to knight as the may go out soon the next morning. Please to let them have strong healthy children as the came at my request (or the wold not have come till the spring).
J. Buns
PS Sr, Should be glad to know whether the old blankets, which the children's clothes came in to me, be required to be sent back or whether I may give them to the nurses. JB

note.value: JOHN COLLET, NEWBURY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: January 7th 1759
Sr

I sent you in a frank last Thursday my last quarterly account to Dec 31 last, which I hope you reced safe. In it I acquainted you of the death of Stephen Pitt, No 4460, who died Jan 2. And enclosed I send up the certificate of his burial and the number that was about his neck, as usual.

I also acquaint you that, having now 105 of the Foundling children under my care, and as the governors owed me last Dec 31 £91 5s 6d, that I intended with their permission (if I heard nothing to the contrary) to draw upon you for £196, payable to Mr Samuel Slocock or order, 21 days after date, which I propose doing next Friday morning, if I hear nothing from you beforehand, and therefore beg leave to give you notice of it now.
I have now sent you (by a nurse of Mr Cates's) my yearly account, together with the nurses' billets and all my receipts etc.
John Collet

note.value: JOHN COLLET, NEWBURY, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD

text.p: Newbury, March 20th 1759
Sr

I am really concerned that I am now to acquaint you of the death of no less than 3 of the foundling children, viz Ann Beddington, No 11920, who died March 18th of a vomiting and looseness which carried her off in 2 or 3 days. This was the child the gentlemen were so good as to give Rachel Edmonds last Tuesday upon my recommendation, and for which I am much obliged to them. I tried rhubarb and the testacea powders with gentle cordials but found but little benefit, but then apprehending that it might be owing to her being weaned too soon, I gave her to a wet nurse to suckle her. She took the breast directly and I was in hopes it would have cured her, but I fear it was tried too late, for she died the next day. I am very sorry I did not try her with the breast at first. The other 2 children are Elizabeth Handy, No 8442, and Thomas Howmark, No 9228, who both of them died yesterday, March 19, of a fever, tho I did the best I could for them.

I recede your letter by nurse Edmonds and have also reced the clothes from Mrs French by the waggon, and please to acquaint her of it, and that the close shifts are of a very good size for the children and fit them very well and are very comfortable to them.
John Collet

note.value: JOHN COLLET, NEWBURY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Newbury, June 24th 1759
Sr

According to your desire I have sent up No 1285, 1296, 1302, 1304, 1325, 1326, 1328, 1329, 1330, 1333 and 1334, being eleven in all. I should have sent Agnes Cock, No 1332, also with them, but as she has been weakly for a great while in her knees, and seems to be now recovering her strength by the use of the cold bath and medicines, I was willing to keep her a few months longer till she was got strong enough to run about, if it is agreeable to the gentlemen of the committee. But if they choose to have her returned to the hospital directly, I will send her up accordingly and therefore desire a line from you about it. Last year Mr Girl, the surgeon, one of the governors of your hospital, was at Newbury when I showed Agnes Cock to him, and consulted him about her and followed his directions, and she is better, though she mends but very slowly. No 1330 has lost one eye which was owing to an inflammation of it when she first came down; and I have formerly informed the hospital of the accident. She has also a weakness of the fundament, which comes down sometimes, but is much better of this disorder than she has been, but I mention it that proper medicines may be given to strengthen that part. Richard Child, 1333, has one leg very weakly but it is better than it was. The rest of the children are pretty well to the best of my knowledge. No 1285, 1304, 1326, 1329, 1330, 1333 and 1334 have had the small pox, as you have justly marked. As to the measles, I never noted it down so am uncertain who have had it and who not; but the nurses tell me that No 1302, 1304, 1325, 1326, 1329 have had that distemper and the nurse of No 1333 has forgot whether he has had it or no. I have sent up only 3 nurses with these children, viz Hannah Wheeler, Margaret Whatley and Mary Chapman, to each of which I would desire the favour of you to give one foundling child to nurse. I should have sent up the rest of the nurses for more children, but my state of health has been but indifferent of late (being naturally of a weak constitution) on which account I am unwilling to increase my number of foundling children but rather a little to lessen them, as I am incapable of giving that attention to them which I ought, but please to present my best compliments to the gentlemen of the committee and assure them that I will take all the care of the children under my inspection that I can and that I am much obligd to them for those which I have.

I have sent you my quarterly account, by which you will see that I make the governors of your hospital indebted to me £53 5s 8d which I hope will prove right. And as I shall have 90 children under my inspection, when these 11 children are gone and three come in their room, I will beg leave to draw in about 12 days upon you for £143, payable to Mr Samuel Slowcock or order, 21 days after date, as usual. Which, if agreeable, be pleased to acquaint me of by these nurses when they return. Three of the children: viz No 1296, 1302 and 1329, have had new shoes about a month or 2 ago, their old ones being quite worn out, but as I have not paid for them yet I shall
insert them in my next quarterly account. I should have given all or most of the others new shoes and also new stockings as theirs are very old but, as they were going up to the hospital, thought it would be better to omit it, as the committee would be best pleased to do it themselves. I shall charge the expenses of carriage of these 3 nurses and the 11 children to my next quarterly account.
John Collet

note.value: JOHN COLLET, NEWBURY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Newbury, September 11th 1759
Sr

I reced the favour of yours, with the opinion of the gentlemen of the committee to allow 3 pence a week for clothing of each child after the first year. This would be extremely agreeable to me as I assure you it is no little trouble I find in this affair of the clothes, and particularly the shoes, which frequently want mending and are often returned to me in half a year or 3 quarters with complaints that they are too little for the children; so that it will be a great ease to me. I have also consulted many of the nurses upon it who are all ready to accept it, provided they may also have the old clothes given to them at the end of the first year, for they say it would be hard upon them to buy new clouts, bay blankets etc at the end of the first year besides the new clothes. So I hope the committee will grant them the old clothes at the end of the year, as they can be of little or no use to any but the nurses. They have also desired me to mention another thing; that as the children may chance to be returned to the hospital when the clothes the nurses have bought for them be but 3, 6 or 9 months old, so they hope that when the children are returned to the hospital, that all their clothes will be returned to the nurses. I beg my best compliments to the gentlemen of the committee and beg the favour of you to communicate to me soon their resolutions upon these 2 points.

As Mary Collins was desirous of giving up her child Erasmus Fleet, No 2122, I removed him Sept 8 last to Elizabet Whore. I shall make up my accounts, and pay the nurses to Sept 29, and then send you up my accounts and the vouchers etc to you the very beginning of October. I very much want some new clothes for several of the children but shall wait till I hear from you, and till it is settled whether the nurses shall buy them or no.
John Collet

If the nurses buy the clothes, would the committee have them have the same sort of linsey coats, or is it indifferent to them what they cloth them in? Mrs Aldworth is gone into the country for a few days, otherwise I should have consulted her, but I believe her nurses are willing to agree to the same terms as mine are.

note.value: JOHN COLLET, NEWBURY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Newbury, November 24th 1759
Sr

This is to acquaint you that Joan Richardson, No 1920, died on Wednesday, Nov 21, of the measles. Sarah Head brought down a fine child, No 14457, for which I thank you. I have recede the parcel of clothes from Mrs Leicester with her letter, but one thing I do not perfectly understand in it, and should be glad of a line from you about it. Are the nurses allowed to keep the old clouts and blankets and pilches as long as thay have the children, or are they to return them to the hospital at all, or no? I used to keep them for a little above 2 years, and then to send them up to the hospital, but I have had great complaints from the nurses for returning them so soon; so beg the favour of your directions and to know whether they may keep them entirely, or only longer than 2 years. As to their old coats and under petticoats, I have always kept them for the nurses to make underpetticoats of the old coats and to keep the children warm. Please to acquaint Mrs Leicester that 12 of these shifts are too small so that the children cannot wear them, and I should be obligd to her if she could send me in a few days 12 close shifts that are as big and as large as the largest she sent me last week and I will return these by the first opportunity, or keep them by me till some others that are younger will want them, which ever she pleases.
John Collet
PS Nov 28. I kept this letter by me till this day as George Robinson, No 13281, was very bad with measles and cutting his teeth at the same time. And I am sorry to acquaint you that he died this day.
Barkham, January 6th 1759
Sir

According to your directions I removed Wm Bayford from Suzanne Allwright as soon as I could find out a proper wet nurse for it out of Mrs Dod's reach,
though I confess I did it with great regret because I believe a better nurse than Suzanne : Alwright has not been recommended to your hospital. The present nurse to Wm Bayford is Susan Giles of Finchampstead in Barks. Since I rec'd yours I have sent one wet nurse and design to send up some more very soon. I know you put out some children to dry nurses and shed therefore be glad to know if my recommendation of one dry nurse wed be acceptable.

Before this last brought home yesterday I hade nineteen children; two of this number died. In the account of nurses sent up by me this last year I have charged but for 14 by Mr Carter and one by Mr Goswell out of 19 nurses. I shall be obliged to you for acquainting me whether all the other 4 nurses carriage were accounted for in the former year or only 2 or 3. I have paid 3 nurses yoir ten shillings each for nursing yoir children a year. Another child has been under my care above a year but, as I was forced to remove that child Juson Balson, No 6656, from Mary Pain to Mary Hill before the year was up, pray tell me whether the 10s be due to Mary Hill now , or not till she has had it a year. I want new clothing for this child and also for 3 more to be sent by Mr Carter of Wokingham.
Wm Daws
NB I mistook your printed letter and settled the accounts with my nurses to the 21st of Decr only and did not see my error till it was too late to account for the remaining 10 days.

note.value: WILLIAM DAWES, BARKHAM, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Barkham, March 19th 1759
Sir

I rec'd the favour of yours but not a word in answer to mine relating to a dry nursed child , nor have you sent the cloths for the seven children under my inspection, who are indeed all in rags. I also desired you to be so kind as to look back to the year '57 and satisfy me how many nurses I had charged the carriage of before the 21st of December 57 because, as I told you, I imagined I had omitted charging 2 nurses or more. Pray send the clothes for 7 children by Carter of Wokingham and let me know whether you can oblige me with one dry nursed child for a good woman I have a regard for. If an inspector at Wokingham be wanting I could recommend Mr Saml Trask of that place as a very honest and substantial tradesman and willing to act in that capacity.
Wm Daws

note.value: WILLIAM DAWES, BARKHAM, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD

text.p: Barkham, April 16th 1579
Sir

When I sent accts at Christmas last to the hospital I desired Mr Colingwood to send me for seven children (above a year old each) 7 suits of cloths. I wrote to Mr Colingwood the second time and he promised to send them very soon. This was about 5 weeks ago, but no cloths are yet come, and most of the nurses are obliged to put on them their own children's cloths, which is very unreasonable without being paid for them. Be pleased therefore to send by Carter this week what cloths I desire or I must buy them here. Martha Gadsby, No 11277, died of a fever April the 12th 1759.
Wm Daws

note.value: WILLIAM DAWES, BARKHAM, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Barkham, April 23rd 1759
Sir

I received the favour of your second letter, relating to a dry nurse child. I gave the woman a recommendation to come to the hospital for it upon receiving your first letter, but the woman fell ill of the rheumatism and depended on Mrs Carter, the Wokingham carrier's wife, to bring the child for her and why she did not, I cannot yet acquaint you. I am very much obliged to you for keeping the child so long and desire you to send the cloths for 7 or 8 children who are now above a year and quarter old and very ragged indeed.
Wm Daws

note.value: WILLIAM DAWES, BARKHAM, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Barkham, July 6th 1759
Sir

Out of the four last children brought from the hospital I gave you notice that two of them were dead and this is to acquaint you with the death of the third: viz Ann Sunbury, No 13159, died July 2nd 1759, and I have prevailed with the nurse of this last to try her luck once more and therefore hope you will be pleased to order for her a child more promising to live. The nurses complain I do not allow them enough to bear yoir charges upon the road and indeed I think so too. Mrs Dod allows each of her nurses 6s. I allow but 2s and 6d in summer and 3s in winter but with your approbation I will give them more, for if any of the children die soon after they have brought them down they are considerable losers, as has been the case of my 3 last nurses. I desire therefore to know what to do in this affair.

I have now near 20 children above a year old and have had cloths for about 10 of them; be pleased to order 7 or 8 sets more by Carter, the Okingham carrier, which, with some of the cloths of the deceased, may serve a good while. The remainder I will return to the hospital. In my last to you, Sir, I hinted my inclination to help a good woman to another dry nursed child as she was a loser by the other, the child dying in about 3 weeks' time and never well whilst she had it.
Wm Daws

note.value: WILLIAM DAWES, BARKHAM, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Barkham, September 14th 1759
Sir

The child Elizabeth Birck delivered to Eliz: Mace Augst First 1759, No 13550, died 12th instant (I imagine of the foul distemper). As the accounts for the children under my inspection are ordered in, I hope you will send some fresh blank receipts before I remit the old ones. I desire also to know what the hospital will allow the nurses for their extraordinary trouble in nursing yoir children in the measels. I believe every foundling under my care has had them.
Wm Daws

NB I do not think 3d a week for yoir cloths sufficient. I have wrote for cloths several times but have recd none yet. I have distributed the cloths of the deceased where most wanted among the living but hope to receive more from the hospital soon.

note.value: JULIANA DODD, SWALLOWFIELD, 1759
TO MR COLLINGWOOD?
SWALLOWFIELD PLACE, JANUARY 23RD 1759

text.p: Sir

I rec'd your letter of the 18th instant by which I find that Mr Naish is indebt'd to me thirty shillings but, as I did not apprehend that his account was wrong at the time I took the children, I gave him a receipt and therefore cannot demand it, nor have I his account to show him; but as I undertake the children for their benefit I do not think thirty shillings of any consequence and therefore only desire a proper discharge to January 1759; and what trifle is due on the balance, deducting the thirty shillings, you will be pleased to send by one of my servants, who shall wait on you for it when I go to London, which will be in a few days.

I must trouble you to inform the matron that, as I leave this place on Sunday next, I must absolutely have some new clothes for the children next week as there are many that cannot leave with out them, and I have already put off going to London some days in order to have some new clothes for the children before I left them. I must also have some magnesia and what was made for a child I sent up last week.
The two following children are dead since Jan the 4th, a male, No 10853, called Paul Bullock and a male, No 10955, called Daniel Ashills.
Juliana Dodd

note.value: JULIANA DODD, SWALLOWFIELD, 1759
TO MR COLLINGWOOD?
CURZON ST, JANUARY 31ST 1759

text.p: Sir

Enclosed is the money that is due from Mr John Naish to the hospital which I rec'd from him on showing Mr Nunns' account. I have also returned you the other papers. I rec'd the clothes etc before I left the country, which were very right. Please to acquaint the steward that I desire to have twenty pounds this day fortnight which I shall send a servant for with a receipt.

I am desired by the Revd Mr Talbot (minister of Burfield, near Reading, Barks), to acquaint you that if it is agreeable to the committee he would like, for the benefit of the children, to have some of them under his care. Therefore, if his offer is accept'd, suppose you will send him the necessary instructions, direct'd as I have mentioned, and I conclude he will send up nurses accordingly. As I am certain he intends to receive no advantage from having the children I wish, for their sakes, he may be accept'd as I think they would be better nursed than under the inspection of a person that has any profit by it; please to acquaint the committee with his offer.
Juliana Dodd

note.value: JULIANA DODD, SWALLOWFIELD, 1759
TO MR COLLINGWOOD?
SWALLOWFIELD PLACE, SEPTEMBER 11TH 1759

text.p: Sir

I rec'd your letter and will return my account the beginning of next month provided you send me some billets time enough. As you desired my opinion in regard to to the clothing of the children I must mention the following objections. In the first place, the nurses inform me that it will cost them seven shillings for the shoes and stockings, one year with a another, from a twelve month old to the time they are returned to the hospital; and the hospital cloths being valued at seven and ninepence it will increase the expense and amount to more than the sum you propose to allow them. Secondly, I fear the nurses are most of them too poor, and not disinterested enough, to lay out the money for the foundlings, only unless by compulsion, which to the inspectors would be infinitely more trouble that that of delivering the cloths. Thirdly, I am afraid their are many of the lower sort of people undertake this office with a view of advantage to themselves, and those people will at all events oblige the nurses so far as to overlook their wanting the decent and necessary cloths to keep them warm and clean, but if the governors have superior reasons to pursue the scheme I will endeavour to prevail on the women to undertake it for the sum.
Juliana Dodd

note.value: JULIANA DODD, SWALLOWFIELD, 1759
TO MR COLLINGWOOD?
SWALLOWFIELD PLACE, SEPTEMBER 23RD 1759

text.p: Sir

I desire I may have sent the new billets for the children under my inspection by the Swallowfield waggon next Friday as I am going from home soon and shall be glad to make up my account and return it before I go, which I can not do unless I have the billets next Friday; and then you shall have my account the week following, which I beg to have a speedy answer to and should be glad to know why they are to be made up before the usual time.

One of the children under my inspection came from the hospital with the itch upon it and has communicated it to the nurse, which is not only a very great disadvantage to her but will also be an expense to have them cured as she has a large family that will, of course, catch it; but I suppose the hospital will pay it, as it is very reasonable they should, and beg to know if I am to charge it or not. I hope there will be more care taken for the future, or I
shall find it difficult to get nurses to send up.
I should be glad to know what Mr Jones of Yately charges for the burials of the children under his inspection, or what the late Mr Nuns did.
Juliana Dodd

note.value: JULIANA DODD, SWALLOWFIELD, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Sir

I reed the billets and would have answered your letter sooner but did not receive it time enough for yesterday's post. I shall send my account to you next Thursday and hope if there is any mistake you will rectify it and let me know by Saturday's post. If not, I hope you will send me the discharge that day as I am going from home for a little time the day following, and beg to receive your answer first as I shall wait the coming in of the post for that purpose.

The reason I desired to know what Mr Jones of Yately charged for the burials was, that you will see by my account, that I have for two children in a neighbouring parish, been obliged to pay a very unreasonable fee which the minister demand'd for signing the certificate, assuring me that Mr Jones never did it under and that the hospital allowed it; but since that I have been informed there is no fee for burring a child that dies in the parish and that they only demand it for signing the certificate, therefore shall have no more buried in the parish where the minister is so exorbitant in his fees. Doctor Collet at Newbury informed me the minister in whose parish he inspected never demand'd anything which, I think, is a proof there is no lawful nor customary fee.
I hope you will be so good to examine my account as soon as you can and let me know by Sunday's post if it is right; if not, what are the mistakes, which will greatly oblige.
Juliana Dodd

note.value: JULIANA DODD, SWALLOWFIELD, 1759 TO THE MATRON
TO MRS FRENCH
SWALLOWFIELD PLACE, DECEMBER 18TH 1759

text.p: Madam

I am informed that the hospital is very full of children and I desired the nurses I sent up last week to inform you that the whooping cough is so very brief here, and so fatal to the children, that it prevent'd me sending more women, as those that offered had it in there familys; but I could recommend some proper dry nurses where the children would be in no danger of catching it, and I am told that there are many in the hospital that are weaned. If so, I desire you will give me leave, by return of the post, to send some dry nurses next week. One at least I desire I may, as I hear other inspectors have had them when they pleased to send for them. I should not ask this if I did not hear that it is usually done by other people. If it is, I expect to have an answer to this by Saturday's post, and the nurse, or nurses, shall be at the hospital the Thursday following.
Juliana Dodd
By the dry nurses I hope you will let me send up next week, I desire you will return me some magnesia.

note.value: WILLIAM EARLES, READING, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Reading, September 2nd 1759
Sr

I recev'd yours dt the 31 August concerning nurse Mary Gibbs. The child I removed from her whas not kepp free from verment and in a verey nasty condishon. Had it remained with her aney longer the child would never had aney use in its limbs. It could stand no more than a feather when taken from her. As for the parson that gave you this information, who the ware, or whether the had ever seen what care this child whas taken of, I should be glad to know.

As for laing them under aney obligation, I never did. As for my one part, I do no business, nor has not for some time past. My soon is in trade. If the lay out aney thing with him, the are welcome. If not, no obligation. I did think of sending up too or three nurses as now being after harvest, but if the gentlemen don't think well of my care, pray send word.
Wm Earls, Inspector
Gentillmen, I shall all ways take care to move those children at my discreson that I know is not well done by. I had given imeadete notis of removing this but was ill.

note.value: WILLIAM EARLES, READING, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD
READING, OCTOBER 8TH 1759

text.p: Sr

I have sent you up those sertifications of the death of those children. I should have sent them sooner but had sent up no nurses and, being ill myself, had laid them by; had for got it, which I hope you will excuse.
Wm Earls

Sir, I shall take it as a faviour if you pleas ask Mrs French to provide me a weaded child or too and I will take care to send up proper nurses to care for them. Please to give an answer by the bearer.

note.value: WILLIAM EARLES, READING, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Reading, October 9th 1759
Sir

I recev'd your letter concerning making up my accounts, which I have sent by the bearer. I have consulted those nurses that have children under my care
concerning clothing those children after the are a year old, and the think the cannot do it under five shilings a quarter. But if the gentlemen don't think well to allow them that, the must comply with your turms. You please to send me word in answer to it because I have some children that now a year old.
Wm Earls

note.value: THOMAS HUBBARD, SONNING, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Sunning, January 20th 1759
Sir

According to your instructions of the 6th inst I have sent up the bearer hereof, John Mattingley, with his wife, nurse Sarah Mattingley, and a child of their own for the purpose and herein mentioned. I should have sent up her nurse child, Tho: Redbourne 7118, too but it is since dead. The disease, we suppose, turned inward, threw the child into strong convulsions and killed it in a few hours. They were all to have set out for London on Tuesday morning last but the child was seized with convulsions on the Monday morning and died before night. I have taken this opportunity to send you my last year's account with the receipts as usual. I have sent up such of nurse Mattingley's child's clothes as are worth returning to the hospital, the year being in a manner expired. Please to desire Mr Blackboard to send me some more blank receipts for the present year and some clothes for Mary Halfacre's nurse child, Philadelphia Scot.
Tho: Hubbard

note.value: THOMAS HUBBARD, SONNING, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD

text.p: Sunning, February 28th 1759
Sir

When John Mattingley and his wife came up to the hospital I sent by them
a parcel directed to Mr Collingwood, the secretary; in which was a letter to him, wherein I desired him to let you know that I wanted some clothes for nurse Mary Halfacre's child and some blank receipts for the current year. But I have not received any such things from you yet, which make me apprehend the said parcel did not come safe to hand. Be pleased to enquire about it and let me know whether it did or not because therein was contained (beside the letter above mentioned) my account for the year 1758 and the certificate of the burial of nurse Mattingley's child Tho: Redbourne. Pray let me have the clothes and receipts above mentioned against Sunday seven-night, for that is my pay day; and then nurse Halfacre may have her child clothes back with her, for she is very impatient and, indeed, her year has been expired almost these two months.
Tho: Hubbard

note.value: THOMAS HUBBARD, SONNING, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD
OCTOBER 23RD 1759

text.p: Sir
I have herewith sent you my account for the Foundling Hospital to the 29 of Septr 1759 with the nurses' receipts, on which are entered all moneys paid for each child, according to instructions.

As to the scheme of allowing the nurses three pence a week to find the children in clothes, I have consulted my nurses upon it, and they and my self are willing to comply with it, if it shall be thought to be for the good of the hospital, and be generally practised. But for my own part, I cannot say I altogether approve of it, for if the allowance is sufficient (which I am in doubt about, as the children grow larger) yet it will be a temptation to the nurses not to keep the children properly clothed; to see which done will give the inspectors a great deal more trouble, in my apprehension, than the present method of sending them a set of clothes once a year, instead of less, as you say the committee apprehend. But, as I said before, I am ready to conform to what ever shall be deemed for the general good of the society. Only I should be glad to know soon what I am to do with respect to such of my nurses whose time is come to have some new clothes, of which I sent Mr Blackboard an account lately, whether they are to have some sent them or whether I am to allow them the extraordinary pay in order to buy them themselves.
Tho: Hubbard

note.value: THEOPHILUS HUGHES, HURST, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD
FEBRUARY 28TH 1759

text.p: Sr

I rec'd yours of the 17th instant on 18th but, it being Sunday, had not time to answer it. And being to set out on a journey next morning early is the reason of lying so long unanswered. My accounts have been drawn out a
considerable time and I was prevented sending them by a multiplicity of family affairs and unforeseen occurrences. Nor can I now send them till next Tuesday by the Ockingham Carrier.

The woman who brings this hath brought one of your children (Benjamin Cox) with the fowl disease and hope you will get her a dry child. It is a pity there have been so many accidents of this kind hereabouts. It must needs be of bad consequence to your nurseries and it always will be so, unless the hospital appoint a proper inspector, and for want hereof many children (I am confident) are lost, by being in a weakly condition sent too long journeys, beyond their strength too bear.

Sr, I desire (if it can be contrived) that there may be sent me by the bearer, nurse Chapman, for Matthew Bruce, No 5642, above 17 months old, a bodice coat and 2 pin cloths. Its nurse hath had shirts and caps already. For Judith Bromley, No 4924, (above 19 months old), a bodice coat; For Lancelot Sims, No 7046, (a very large child, tho but just turned of 12 months old), a bodice coat, also a bodice coat and linen of all sorts for the following children vizt :
for Ann Weaverly, No 6320, (above 15 months old)
for Jacob Adams, No 5643, (above 17 months old)
for Geoffrey Bell, No 6819, (above 14 months old)
for Lawrence Penny, No 7049, (above 13 months old)

for Eleanor Ralphson, No 5761, (above 17 months old) If they can be sent by the bearer, it will save the expense of carriage; otherwise please to let them be got ready against the Ockingham carrier brings my accounts next week. I should be sorry if my accounts came too late to be settled this year.

But one thing I must request your direction in, namely whether I must return to the hospital all the old and useless rags I receive from the nurses in exchange for the new things. If I am to return them you must take them by the lump, for I have not time to take an account of the separate parcels.
I earnestly beg the favour of your putting the enclosed unto the penny post as soon as possible.
The: Hughes
The bearer hath two pence for the penny post - ask her for it.

note.value: THEOPHILUS HUGHES, HURST, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD

text.p: Sr

I rec'd the favour of yours by the nurse last Saturday and pray my compliments to Mrs French and tell her I will have a watchful eye over the child according to her desire. You herewith receive in a sack all the clouts (not already returned) belonging to the children that died last year, as also the old things rec'd on the delivery of the new. Pray send me down the clothes I wrote for last Wednesday by Chapman, the nurse of the child returned with the fowl disease.

I have hitherto brought white yarn stockings for all my children but should be glad to know for the future, after I have disposed of those in hand, which sort would be most agreeable to the hospital, white yarn or speckled worsted. In the same sack are my accounts and hope thay will come soon eno' to be passed; and trust to Mr Collingwood's perusal of them, being a very bad accountant myself and having not the help at hand I had last year to adjust them for me.

NB My respects to Mr Collingwood and acquaint him that the balance in my name at the expiration of last year is, by my accounts, above £100. I have made 2 months' payments to all my nurses since to the 25th of last inclusive which, with rewards and other incidents and charges, amount to above £80. Nothing more occurs to me at present but that.
The: Hughes

note.value: THEOPHILUS HUGHES, HURST, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD
MARCH 30TH 1759

text.p: I desire you to forward with what speed you can the clothes I sent by my last nurses, as also the two suits I wrote for in my lrtt to Mr Collingwood yesterday, with one whole suit more for Sarah Garland, No 7812, about 13 mo old. Please to send them by Jno Carter, the Oakingham waggoner, and whereas I see by a lertt I rec'd from Mr Collingwood that I had charged paid to Mary Grout twice over in the same duplicate, 2 March 1758, 10s for the same month's wages. Please to see and send me word whether I have not omitted 10s, 2d March, in her other duplicate belonging to her other child under her care; otherwise I can't conceive how I could make such a horrid blunder. Please also to send me word what stockings the hospital allows their children, whether white yarn or coloured worsted. Another thing I want very much to be informed of is, whether a nurse that takes a child that is removed from its first nurse is entitled to the reward of 10s after having it a whole year under her care, in case the first nurse did not keep it long eno' to be entitled to the reward. Your answer to these queries will oblige.
The: Hughes

note.value: THEOPHILUS HUGHES, HURST, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD
SEPTEMBER 13TH 1759

text.p: Sr

I rec'd the favour of yours subjoined to Mr Collingwood. My accounts shall be sent up by the time directed. Pray tell me the reason of this new regulation. I have mentioned the hospital's proposal to all my nurses about clothes, who are willing to accept thereof on condition it takes place from the first day of next January and they have the liberty to retain the old clothes to mend, what they buy, when wanted. I am of opinion it will serve all ends. In the next place, Sr, please to consult Mr Collingwood whether the nurses that have had children a whole year from other nurses, from whom I removed them for neglect before they were entitled to the reward, ought not to be paid the reward when they have taken care of them for a year, and favour me with his answer by the bearer. I have sent you up 5 nurses and shall send you up a few more next week in hopes they will meet more candid treatment from the present matron than they did from Mrs French and her sister. A nurse of mine, Eliz: Ann Chapman, who sometime since brought you Benjn Cox with the fowl disease, desires the favour of a dry child to make her amends for the trouble etc she had with that child. A reasonable request, I think; and hope you will be so good as to forward her petition as soon as opportunity offers. Pray give me a line.
The Hughes

note.value: THEOPHILUS HUGHES, HURST, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD
OCTOBER 4TH 1759

text.p: Sr

Whereas Mr Collingwood's directions as to send my accounts to the 29th of Sepr, I must desire you to inform me by Saturday's post, without fail, whether he means inclusive, or exclusive, of that day. And whereas he farther directs the vouchers for my payments to be transmitted, together with said accounts, before the end of this instant October (which shall be punctually done) and underneath said order is printed: 'NB By the vouchers are meant the nurses' receipts, on the back of which are to be entered all the monies paid on account of each child.'

I desire farther to know whether I am to transmit only the sd account of monies by me paid to the respective nurses, with their receipts for such payments, for the inspectors of the Parliament or whether I am not, at the same time, to transmit an account of all other monies by me expended on the foundling children, with the several vouchers, or whether this last account is to be deferred to the end of this year, 1759. Pray don't fail answering these two questions by Saturday's post. For the printed directions sent by Mr Collingwood, Septr the 8th, are very obscure and need explanation.

NB My nurses who have had children under their care for a year, taken from bad nurses, who have received no reward, think themselves entitled for the whole reward of 10s and desire me to represent the hardship of the contrary, as it may be reasonably presumed they must have had more trouble with such children than if they had taken them at first out of the hospital, and further say that, had not been for the prospect of the reward at the end of their having had them a year, they would not have taken that extraordinary trouble upon them, and indeed I think their expectation well grounded, not only for the reason they give, but also because of the printed rules of your hospital, among which I find that every nurse who takes due care of a child for a year shall have 10s for her care thereof as a reward, which I think must mean a reward for every nurse for a child for whom a reward hath not been paid before. And as it is material that I should have an answer to make before I close my accounts, pray my due respects to Mr Collingwood and consult him hereon, that I may also have an answer hereto at the same time.
The: Hughes

note.value: THEOPHILUS HUGHES, HURST, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD
OCTOBER 7TH 1759

text.p: Sr

I observe what you say about the resolution of your committee on 11th Jany 1758. In answer whereto I think I may justly urge that all private rules and orders relating to nurses under inspectors and subsequent to the general printed rules and orders of your house delivered to us for our instruction on our commencing inspectors, ought not in equity to take place till after such subsequent resolutions and orders are notified to all parties concerned therein,
that they may act accordingly. Dry children are a favour but this is not always the case of children removed from one nurse to another, nay, tic oftener otherwise; and he must be very base and mean-spirited that removed a child with the view you mention, a charge on the inspectors in general that ought not to be so much as intimated unless you had flagrant proof of such instances. In which case the guilty ought to be accused and cashiered with the utmost infamy and disgrace.

And in my humble opinion, were more children weaned as soon as they came to your hands, so many half starved babes would not be sent into the country, and nurses would be easier had, and I don't see but that, generally speaking, children bred up by hand do full as well as those that have the breast. Sure I am they are not liable to so many ills as in all probability they are subjected to from nurses in the hospital, where there is sometimes such scarity of nurses that you must, of course, take any that can be got.
The: Hughes

note.value: THEOPHILUS HUGHES, HURST, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD
OCTOBER 11TH 1759

text.p: Sr
I desire to know by Saturday's post without fail whether 2 or 3 nurses can be furnished with children in case I send them up next Tuesday or Wednesday.

Please to acquaint Mrs Brookes that on Septr 17th last Jane New had with Samuel Osgood, No 13946, three caps, 2 shirts and 5 clouts very old and two bad a great deal to be charged at the price the nurses takes them at, or to be of much service. Tic pity the parcel of clothes are not opened and told over to each nurse, that they may see what they have before they reach the country. Another of my nurses that had a child on the 14th Dc, and which child was buried on the 29th Dcr, was served the same. This is a stale trick of the nurses in the hospital, who are used to keep the good things for themselves and put the country nurses off with others too bad to answer the end. I desire to know whether Mrs Brooke sees the clothes before they are bundled up, for I shall certainly send these things up for the inspection of the hospital, being unwilling that my nurses should be thus imposed on.

Pray do you know what the Parliament is about? I see in the papers 3 pamphlets advertised against your hospital by one Massy. I wish you would send them me down by my first nurses, them comes who shall bring you money to pay for them. I am informed they trying to put a stop to taking in any more children.
You shall be sure to have my accounts in due time.
The: Hughes

note.value: THEOPHILUS HUGHES, HURST, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD
OCTOBER 30TH 1759

text.p: Sir

One of the last 3 weakly children I had from the hospital is dead, and another expected to die every hour, so desire to know by Thursday's post if I can be supplied with 2 or 3 children next Monday. I must also desire you to send me down, as soon as you can, a suit of clothes for Wm Archer, No 5012, above 2 years old, under Ann Cotton; ditto for Mary Dawson, No 5640, above 2 years old under ditto ; ditto for Hy Anderson, No 8894, above 16 mo old, Ruth Burgess nurse; ditto for Elijah Gale, No 10058, above a year old, Rachael Payne nurse; ditto for John Ponsonby, No 9673, above a year old, Elizth Breach nurse; ditto for Nathanl Pilchard, No 9579, above a year old, Elizth Allaway nurse; ditto for Jocelyn Dracker, No 8972, above 16 mo old, nurse Elizth Clarke. Be so good as to send these cloths with speed, being much wanted.

I sent my accounts a fortnight ago, but on perusal of one of the apothecary's bills (who hath a number of foundlings under his care), finding several charges therein which did not belong to my children, I was obliged to return to him his bill to rectify it, and could not get it again till yesterday. I will send them again tomorrow morning by the Reading Machine without fail; so hope they will be with you about 4 o'clock, but cannot send up the certificates of the burials till you send me some printed forms, which please to do by my nurses next week.

Amongst my receipts for rewards paid there may, for ought I know, be one or two rewards for a whole year to the second nurse for children removed from a bad nurse who had no premium , but this happened to be paid before I knew of the rule, made since the printed orders for paying it were sent to me in 1756 when I first commenced inspector. And indeed, as I knew nothing of the resolution of the committee of 11 Jany 1758 to the contrary, till informed thereof by Mr Collingwood, Octr the 6th instant, I don't see how it can, or ought to, bind me or my nurses for what was done that date. That resolution should have been printed and sent to every inspector as soon as taken. Indeed Mr C. saith that I may observe thereby many inconveniences are prevented, but mentions only one: vizt , an inspector's taking a child from its first nurse and giving it to a 2nd favourite nurse just before the reward was due on purpose that she might have the reward.

Now indeed your hospital has reasons to suspect their inspectors guilty of a low base and unjust action, such a rule might prevent the injustice done hereby to the first nurse, supposing the 2nd was to receive the reward as soon as the child was a year old. But that is not my care. I propose only the 2nd nurse being paid the reward after she hath it under her care a whole year, and no reward given to the first, and the child taken from the first for
notorious neglect. So that here can be no partiality in favour of that 2nd nurse who might be entitled to a premium as soon by being recommended to the hospital for a child thereout.

This is the only inconvenience he mentions, which I show is none at all. He then adds 'dry children are a favour', ie supposing children removed to be all so. But that is, I believe, to be seldom the case. I am sure it is not so with me. For out of 9 children removed by me, there could be but 2 dry children, which were Jno Wigmore, No 6097, and Noah Watkins, whose number I have forgot, it being dead and the paper returned last year. These two children were taken out of the hospital by Mary Norton, Octr 26 1757, and removed to Mary Butcher, October 17 1758, and the reason of removing them was notorious for the whole neighbourhood, vizt , Noah Watkins having received such a contusion under its breast almost big eno' to thrust the fist into and a total neglect of it, it being a black, and of this contusion it languished and soon died after its removal. The other were removed as I saw fit, some at 1 age, some at another, none above half a year old, so not weaned and could be no favour to the 2nd nurse.

Now how these nurses, babes or self can be deemed to fall under the resolution of 11 of Jany 1758, as Mr Collingwood explains it, I cannot see. It is true the committee have a right to make and repeal what rules they please. But then immediate notice thereof ought to be given to those whose actions are to be regulated thereby. And till such notice, I humbly insist such resolutions, or orders, or rules (call 'em what you please) can be of no force, and therefore I hope, as I knew nothing thereof till the 6th instant, you will not make me forfeit my promise to my nurses, nor deprive them of their expected reward at the expiration of their having these removed children a whole year, as expressed in the former printed rules sent me in 1756. My nurses will, none of them, take less than the whole reward, but insist on the whole from me, according to my declaration to them at their taking them, who knew nothing of any subsequent resolution to the contrary, and I am in honour bound to pay them, being fully persuaded that they would not have taken them, were it not in expectation of the reward, there being much more care and trouble to be bestowed on abused children than ordinary. Pray let this be stated to your committee and favour me with your answer.
Of what my respective children have died, etc, you shall hear as soon as I have printed certificates.
Wrote in haste.
The: Hughes

note.value: NOTE WRITTEN OUTSIDE

text.p: This was intended to have been sent to you by last night post but the post going by me, without calling as usual at my gate, I lost that opportunity.

note.value: THEOPHILUS HUGHES, HURST, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD

text.p: December 4th 1759
Sir

Mr Collingwood having been so kind as to inform me by his letter last Sunday that I might have a dry child if I would send quickly for it, I have recommended the bearer accordingly and take this opportunity of desiring the following clothes, as soon as possible vizt :

For Ann Weaverly, No 6320, above 2 ire old, a whole suit (Eliz Church, nurse); ditto for Judith Bromly, No 4924, age ditto , (Mary Mural, nurse); ditto for Those Orange, No 5014, age about 2 yrs and half old, ditto for Jno Wigmore, No 6097, age 2 yrs and 2 mo old, (Mary Butcher, nurse); ditto for Joan Cabot, No 8702, a ire old the 15 instant, (Ann Lewis nurse).

And here I can't but complain to you that whereas I did on the 30th of Octr last write for 7 whole suits, and did accordingly about the middle of Novr (after my pay day on the 4th was past) receive by the Reading Machine a bundle of clothes (which hath ever since been under my own lock and key, unpacked), on unpacking the same on Monday last, being pay day, in order to distribute them, to my great surprise, I found 12 caps instead of 21. Wherefore, with my respects to Mrs Lister, please to acquaint her herewith that she see where the fault lies and desire her to send me down 9 caps more with the above clothes, which I request may be before my next pay day on the 30th instant.

And here I can't omit acquainting you that whereas I did, some time in the beginning of Octr or latter end of Septr, write to the committee in behalf of some of my nurses, setting forth their hardship of not being allowed the reward for children moved from bad nurses (who had not on that account had them a year and were not therefore entitled to any reward) after the 2d nurses had taken care of 'em for a whole year. Mr Collingwood sends me a copy of their order empowering me to pay the reward to only two of these second nurses, so that my letter hath been greatly mistaken by them, I having applied for their leave to give it to them all - and there is as much reason for all as for two: vizt both their and my ignorance of any private order of the house to the contrary, and for that they would not have taken them under their care, had it not been for the expectation of the reward and for that I am bound in honour to pay it to them out of my own pocket, if the hospital will not having (to induce them to take these children from the bad nurses under their care) told them that at the end of their having them a full year, they would be entitled to the reward. Pray be so good as to impart this, with my respects, to Mr Collingwood and request him to lay my letter, if in being a 2nd time, before the committee and that he would be so good as to impart their final resolution thereon to me. NB Mr Collingwood hath the no and names of these children with their 1st and 2nd nurses' names, and the time of their removal, and I don't know if
any of 'em were weaned; and am confident there could not be above 1 or 2 at most weaned, if any, but only believe not one.
The: Hughes

note.value: JOHN PRICE JONES, YATELEY, 1759
TO MR COLLINGWOOD?
YATELY, MAY 22ND 1759

text.p: Sir

I am informed there is one Withe, a little ale house keeper in this neighbourhood, has solicited the governors for the care of some of the children belonging to the late Mr Nunns' list. As I intend to devote great part of my time to the service of the poor children, I with willingly give up none that Mr Nuns inspected. Three or four nurses from Heckfield came here yesterday and said they are too well acquainted with Mr Withe's character to expect good usage from him and therefore declared they had much rather come to Yately as usual for their money, though they are his next door neighbours, as it were. I shall only beg leave to add that I shed be very sorry to hear he has any of the foundling children under his care, for I can very well foresee what with be the consequences of it. I have taken the liberty to say this merely from a principle of humanity and the desire I have to see justice done the poor children.
Jno P. Jones

note.value: JOHN PRICE JONES, YATELEY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD
YATLEY, JUNE 30TH 1759

text.p: Sir

The smallpox is just got among some of the foundling children under my inspection. I have ordered proper care to be taken of them, with an apothecary to attend those where the symptoms are dangerous. I shall shortly give you a list of their names. I make it my business often to ride round to see all the children, except a few at the distance of twelve miles, whom I find very inconvenient to visit as often as I cd wish, and the nurses complain it is no less fatigueing to them to bring them to me. I shall therefore order them to surrender up the children to me and I will take care to provide nurses within my reach upon whose conduct and care of poor children I may safely depend.
John P. Jones

note.value: JOHN PRICE JONES, YATELEY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD
AUGUST 22ND 1759

text.p: Sir

You'll please to order a parcel of certificates for me this week. I want some of both sorts but one of the nurses will bring them. Pray, Sir, is there some consideration made by the hospital to such nurses, where the children happen to be claimed by the parents, besides the ordinary allowance, I mean, for their journey. I hope I shall not be exposed to the inconvenience of waiting any longer for the clothes.

One of the children is afflicted with the worms to such a degree that its belly and other parts are swelled to an imensense size. I wish something may be done for its relief. For my part I shall not venture upon any thing before I have proper instructions from you what to do.
John P. Jones

note.value: JOHN PRICE JONES, YATELEY, 1759
TO MR COLLINGWOOD?
YATELY, SEPTEMBER 9TH 1759

text.p: Sir

I reed your favour of the 5th instant. I have mentioned to as many of my nurses as I've since meet with the proposal which was made to me by the hospital, viz , that they are for the future to provide clothes for your children after the 1st year, upon being allowed 13s a year for it and, as far as I can find, they are all very well satisfied. As for myself, tic certain I have nothing to object to it. When the scheme has taken place all that I have to do is to see, as near as I can, that justice be done the poor children, and I must be particularly circumspect in it. The nurses beg that the old clothes may not be returned because, though they can be but of little service to the hospital, yet may be very useful to them. I have hitherto referred the article of providing shoes and stockings for the children to my deputy, as Mr Nuns used to do before me, but upon examining particularly into their several prices at the shops I have found, to my great surprise, that my predessessor and this very man (who was also his deputy) did all along greatly impose on the hospital. I have, therefore, for that and some other reasons discharged him.

Mrs Roberts, a very worthy, good lady in this neighbourhood, has been so obliging as to offer me all the assistance in her power; she has been already very kind and tender to many of the poor children upon several occasions. I shall account with the hospital, according to the time which you have appointed. I rec'd the cloths this day.
John P. Jones

note.value: JOHN PRICE JONES, YATELEY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD
YATELEY, SEPTEMBER 14TH 1759

text.p: Sir
Fourteen days hence I shall draw on the hospital for one hundred pounds, payable at sight to Mr Edward Meal, for the use of the foundling children under my inspection.

The children are most of them in very good health; one indeed has the French disorder pretty bad and I'm somewhat apprehensive it may have given it its nurse, though as yet no symptom of it have appeared on her. There's another, which was brought down about six weeks ago, has a most inveterate sort of itch, which it has given to its nurse and all the rest of the family. The poor people are greatly alarmed at so malignant a distemper. I have ordered an apothecary to attend them.
John P. Jones

note.value: JOHN PRICE JONES, YATELEY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Yately, November 13th 1759
Sir

The nurse whom I mentioned to you some time ago to have returned without a child was not herself a wet nurse but the child was to have been suckled all the way down by a couple of wet nurses who came down in the waggon with her and when it was, to have been given to an excellent wet nurse that I had ready for it. I gave the poor woman five shillings towards repaying the expenses of her journey, with which she seemed very well contented. If what I did was not right I can easily remedy it. I have been so much importuned by a wet nurse that I have given her a certificate this week but on condition she is to bear her expenses if the hospital can't furnish her with a child.
John P. Jones

note.value: JOHN PRICE JONES, YATELEY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: November 28th 1759
Sir

Fourteen days after date, I shall draw on the hospital for one hundred pounds, payable to Mr Edward Meal, for the use of the foundling children under my inspection. My last draught on the hospital, being honoured a full week later than it ought to have been, occasioned me an excessive deal of fatigue. For to save the poor creatures the fruitless trouble of coming for their pay at the usual time, I was obliged to go round them all in order to appoint another day for paying them. My method is, Sir, to draw for money a week before it is due to the nurses; that so I may have that space of time to get it changed, which generally proves a difficult piece of work here in a country place. For my part, I choose never to have more money in my hands than just what I have immediate occasion for.

I shd be glad to have some more chilcane and crabs' claw powders. The child Mordecae Jones, No 13733, is removed form Hannah Packer of Farnboro', Hints to Mary Elms of Ash, Surry and the child David Vinks, No 9823, is removed to from Mary Spencer of Eversley to Frances Darney of Heckfield, Hints. Both the said children were removed by reason of their being extremely ill-used by their former nurses.
John P. Jones

note.value: JOHN PRICE JONES, YATELEY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: December 20th 1759
Sir

The nurses Anne Girdler and Suzanne Catter, two whom I had recommended to you this week, had a child each from the hospital about a month ago but have had the ill luck to lose them both some time since of a violent purging and vomiting. What the nature of the distemper was I know not, but it certainly was in some degree infectious; for two other children whom the same nurses suckled caught it and died a few days after, with the same symptoms upon them the others had. I can very safely affirm that the poor infants wanted nothing their nurses or myself thought necessary for their good.
John P. Jones

PS The child Patience Harrison, No 13849, is removed from Patience Higgs of Stratfield Sea , Hints, to Ann Maynard of Yately, Hints, on account of the former being with child and the infant being too young to be weaned.

note.value: JAMES KENTING, EASTHAMPSTEAD, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD
EASTHAMPSTEAD, MARCH 11TH 1759

text.p: Sir

This is to acquaint you that I cannot possible execute the office of a inspector, for I am not in the business as I was and for me to trouble myself with things without any profit, it is hurtful, for I understand there is nothing allowed from the hospital to any inspector, and likewise I have no regulations in no respect for to go by. I have recovered none from Mrs Dryden's assestor, if she had any. These papers and eleven pounds nine shillings and sixpence I received. The nurses wanted their money and they went to Carter the waggoner and asked him who're I might not pay them, and he told them that I might pay them, and I have paid ten pounds to the nurses and I have one pound nine shillings and sixpence in hand, and there is two children dead, one before I received the things and one since. The childring's names I do not know. There is no demand made for the charges of the burals unless the clark, four shillings for his charges, but if you please to let me know where I may pay it or I no, I will pay it or if you please to send for it by any one, they may have it.
Jose Kenting

note.value: JAMES KENTING, EASTHAMPSTEAD, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Barks Easthampstead, September 9th 1759
Sir

In answer to the proposal in your last letter concerning the nurses 3 pence per week, I have consulted with the nurses and some thinks it may be done for the same, and other some thinks it cannot be done for it to discharge a Christian part by them, and I am of the same opinion that it cannot be done for so little; for understand the childring will remain under the care of their nurses for the space of four or five years before called for. For you may easily judge with yourselves that, as they grows up, they will want more clothes, which will be a bigger charge to the nurses or to you. But I most easily think that they will keep them clothed for the same before they will part with them. But in regard to your judging that it will be an easiment to the inspectors, I doe easily apprehend it will not, for reason the nurses will be dillitry in clothes for them and then the inspector must inspect into it, and they will say they have a proper allowance to cloth them; and so the insp may doe little thing else then remove them from one place to a another, etc.

But in regard to the making up the accounts, I will make them up and send them up in October and I will give you a true account of every farthing
I have disbursted, and likewise the money I have in hand I will return to you, or to whom so ever you will direct. For if you doe not think well of my inspection, I will resin it up whenever you please, and so I desire your answer to it.
Jose Kenting, inspector

note.value: JAMES KENTING, EASTHAMPSTEAD, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD

text.p: Barks Easthampstead, October 6th 1759
Sir

I recede the papers and the letters and I have sent up the accounts according as you desired. There is a mistake in Mrs Povye's raised , for I dated the wrong paper for the child that died last, but I was not willing to alter it because you might think it to wrong you, but I did not.

Likewise the clerk's accounts is not a like. The first bill I paid him double dues and I did not like it and he said that Mrs Dryden paid him double dues always, but ours is a free burying place and if a child has been in the place 40 days hee gains a burial, and so the last bill I paid him 2 shillings and I never will pay him more, and if I have made any mistake I will right it according to your desire, for I ham consious and free from wronging you of anything.

According to the close of the accounts I have mad £63 11s 4d. I rec'd of Mrs Dryden £11 9s 6d, deduct £1 7s 11d, then there is £10 1s 7d. Mrs Dryden's anssessors and I have some dealings to gether. They owes me £11 15s, and when we ballonces we will out set it, if you think well of it. I have reed £90 1s 7d of your hospital so if there is any thing that is not right, pray let me know and I will rectfie it.
Jose Kenting
A list of the childring now a live:
Sarah Boyer has Arabella Frew

Sarah Slark has Matthew Lambet and Maercy Hartley Elizabeth Giles has Willm Willis
Sarah Povey has David Garrick
Hannah Shorter has Easter Travel
Hannah Mepham has Sarah Lawson
Ann Cotterell has Luciah Smith and Jasper Hall Eleanor Cock has Elizabeth Frame and Catherine Yarmouth

note.value: JAMES KENTING, EASTHAMPSTEAD, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Barks Easthampstead, October 7th 1759
Sr

Please to let me know your mind concerning the nurses finding the childring clothes after the first year, for their be some of the childring that has wanted clothes for some time and the nurses are displeased because I doe not let them know what they are to doe for clothes. So if your minds is fixed up on the affair, that is, where the nurses are to find them clothes or not etc. I have proposed it to the nurses and some are willing and some not and so let me know your minds and according to your desire it shall be done with the outmost dispatch etc. I understand the matron, Mrs French, is gone and so I know not how to send for clothes without your letting me know how to direct.
Jose Kenting, inspector
February 5th 1759
Mr Blackboard

My missing in my acct his own to my two much business. Nurse Chalton from 16 Feby to the 30 Decr is only 6 weeks short of the year so it must come to £5 15s, so that it's not 10s over. As to nurse Tompson, if the washing money be pt in both receipts, it's my mistake, for I pt but for Rodger Phillips, 5543. As to nurse Plant, in maken up in a hurry I did not observe I had charged 18s 10d twice, so I must desire you to make up the account as you find it, and send it down directly, for I have pt 5 weeks since. My business to my day servants cause me to pay a least £300 a year, and the fatigue of that and yours is rather to much for me, as I am under some disorder of body.
T. Marsham

note.value: THOMAS MARSHAM, READING, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD
READING, JULY 15TH 1759

text.p: Sr

One of my nurses, Ann Hearth, whom I indulged to carry back a child which had a disorder in its head, and took back John Minshall, No 12693, May 8th, has by his ill manaigement obliged me to propose removing it to Jane Dell that had to nurse Letticha Fleming, a black since dead, and she have lately laying-in and is a good nurse. But yesterday this Ann Heath refused to deliver the child, but swears she will carry it back to the Hosptall, and very likely she will by coatch tomorrow. If so, I hope you will find some way to punish his and I will send up the said Jane Dell for the same child, but that expense is 9s which may be saved and I have some reason to believe some of the clothing is made away with.
T. Marsham
PS I had no answer to my last abt Mrs Compton

note.value: THOMAS MARSHAM, READING, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD
READING, JULY 21ST 1759

text.p: Sr

I sent up my year's acct the 2d of Jouly, in a sack of returned close of children dead. I fear it did not come to your hand as I have no word of its being posed in 3 weeks. Since that I have buried No 8145, Littisha Flemon, a black, with the meazells which is with us very mortal. We had several had the small pox and all did well but one. I get the advise of Mr Hawks, my apothecary, in difficael ceases for I think children should not be quite neglected after so much expense. I am not much concerned at the death of this child, being so very ordinary, but the death of others affect me very much. In my letter some time ago I informed you that Mr Barlow refused to sign the certificate of burying without 1s which was not demanded by the minister for Sonning, Cavsham, Tilhurst nor Heckfield (nor of him before). If I am to pay it, let me know. My sack was left for 2nd cloths for 10 children or 12.
T. Marsham

note.value: WILLIAM NUNNS, YATELEY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Sir

I have sent you some wet nurses and shall send more next week unless you forbid it. I find by the nurses that Mrs Dodd hath been supplied with two or more dry nursed children. I expected by your letter that every inspector was to be supplied by rotation. I have had none for above this half year. Be pleased to acquaint Mr Secretary Collingwood that Conrad Ross, No 6691, and Mary Drake, No 7772, have lately had the measles and are recovered. Be pleased likewise to inform him that if my account sent to him, upon examination, proves right I hope he will send me a proper discharge for the same, with the balance settled to the 31st of December 1758. Be pleased to inform the matron that I received the clothes, and that the clothes next month will be wanting for the following children, namely: One year old:

note.value: LIST OMITTED

text.p: Wm Nuns

note.value: WILLIAM NUNNS, YATELEY, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD
YATELY, FEBRUARY 14TH 1759

text.p: Sir

I desire you would give the enclosed to Mrs French. I have sent you several wet nurses and shall send you more next week. Be pleased to present my compliments to Mr Secretary Collingwood and inform him that I have received his discharge and that the balance for the receipt of money from the steward is estimated to the 3rd of January 1759. It is a pleasure to me to find that I can be any ways instrumental in promoting so laudable a charity and that my accounts of disbursements meet with the approbation of the committee.

I have a case to be laid before the worthy members of the committee in order for their instructions therein. A nurse lately under my inspection who had a child from the hospital three months last past, but is now dead, applied to me this week with a sore breast by direction of an apothecary at Oakingham, Barks, who told her that the foundling was infected with the Lues Venery and had communicated the same to her, which was the occasion of her sore breast. She strongly insisted that I should pay for the
cure of the said breast. I told her I had no such commission from the hospital, nor would I act without, and bid her be gone with her impertinence, and told her if the hospital was to relieve every nurse with a sore breast their expenses would be considerably augmented. She then urged that he had cured three nurses of the said malady by order of one Mr Buns, a tallow chandler and grocer of Oakinham, Barks, who were under his inspection (but I presume only as a deputy) at the expense of the hospital. Now I desire to know whether the said Mr Buns hath any such commission from the hospital to act in this manner. I shall wait for the resolution and instruction of the committee and do nothing farther in this affair till then.
Wm Nuns

note.value: WILLIAM NUNNS, YATELEY, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD
YATELY, FEBRUARY 21ST 1759

text.p: Sir

The nurse who nursed the lame child, James Archer, No 2425, returns you thanks and is very willing to have her child again, but being a little indisposed, hath desired and procured the bearer of this, Elizabeth Mitchel, to bring the child for her. I desire you would be so kind as to deliver the said child to Elizabeth Mitchel and fill up the billet with the nurse's name, of which you will receive a certificate, and I will take care the nurse shall sign the billet here. I shall send more nurses up the next week. I have inquire'd more perfectly into the affair of the nurse's breast which I desired might be laid before the committee and find, by the best esteemed in practice, that it proceeded from a venereal taint in the child.

I have two nurses now labouring under the same malady, who are really objects of compassion, who do not only suffer the grief and anguish of their breasts, but the taunts and reproaches of their neighbours. I hope if the committee allow any inspector to relieve in the said complaint, they will allow me. If not, I shall not have it in my power to send any more nurses to the hospital. Be please'd to remind Mrs French to send the clothes as soon as possible.
Wm Nuns

note.value: WILLIAM NUNNS, YATELEY, 1759 TO MR BLACKBEARD
NO DATE

text.p: Sir

I have sent you some wet nurses but the case of the nurses' breasts hath alarmed the country so much that I cannot procure so many as I might have done otherwise. Be pleased to inform Mr Secretary Collingwood that I
received his letter of 25th instant wherein was contained the order of the committee about the nurse's breast but, Newbury being at 20 miles distance from this place, I am afraid the nurses will not comply with the order on that account. There is at Oakingham, about six miles distant, one Mr Wilmot, an experienced surgeon, and regularly bred. One of the nurses' breasts is perfectly cured, and I desire to know whether the committee will be pleased to order me to pay any money to the surgeon or nurse for the cure.

I have placed Jones Archer, No 2425, the lame child, with Lydia Moore of Yately, DN, because his quondam nurse hath an infamous character. I have likewise removed William Tyrrel, No 8170, the ruptured child, from Sarah Duffin of Eversly Hints, WN, but a very bad one, to Jane Othen of Yately, Hints, DN, a very good one. I shall be very desirous of the farther orders of the honourable committee. Remind the matron concerning the clothes.
Wm Nuns

note.value: MRS SPENSE, SWALLOWFIELD, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Blackheath November 5th 1759
Sir

I now send you my account for the year up to Michaelmass, which I make no doubt will prove right. I should have sent it to you much sooner but I have been prevented by material business which has called me at different times out of town.

All the children under my care are as well, as I was informed last Friday. My nurses live in the parish of Swallowfeild and Arborfeild in Berkshire. I shall be obliged to you if you will acquaint Mrs Brook that I have two nurses coming up this week from Swallowfeild. The will return back on Friday; that the may be provided with children for them to take down with them.

I have been a long time promised a dry nurse child and, as soon as it may suit that I may have one, shall be obliged to you to let me know by a line or two a week beforehand. It is for a nurse that has had a great deal of truble with the children. I am willing to make her some amend by that means as it will be acceptable to her.
E. Spense

note.value: GEORGE TALBOT, BURGHFIELD, 1759 TO MR COLLINGWOOD

text.p: Burfield near Reading, Barks, June 12th 1759 Sir

In pursuance of the directions in a printed letter contained in the packet sent to me from the hospital, this is to inform you that it is indebted to me to the sum of thirteen guineas.
